# HAIR

> HAIR is a Home Assistant custom integration (HACS-compatible) that provides a
> full admin UI for infrared device management.
> Built on top of HA's native infrared platform (introduced in HA 2026.4), HAIR
> handles capturing, fingerprinting, deduplicating, organizing, and transmitting
> IR commands through a single sidebar panel at /hair. No YAML, no manual entity
> definitions, no automations required for basic IR device control.

HAIR sits between the user and HA's IR platform. It does not replace IR hardware
integrations (Broadlink, ESPHome, etc.). It complements them by providing the admin
layer those integrations lack -- analogous to how Z-Wave JS UI manages Z-Wave
devices on top of the Z-Wave JS integration.

Key components:

- HAIR Sniffer: a passive listener that captures every IR transmission seen by
  configured receivers, fingerprints each signal using short/long pulse-duration
  analysis, deduplicates repeated presses, filters out repeat frames (sent when
  buttons are held), and groups signals by source remote based on carrier frequency
  and preamble analysis. All in real time. Any signal can be given an alias (a
  user nickname that replaces the diamond pattern in the UI); an alias is a label
  on the signal, not a command name. Remotes, and the signals within a remote, can
  be drag-reordered; the order is persisted (it replaced the old hit-count sort),
  and a newly seen remote or signal surfaces at the top until the user moves it.
  A signal's raw Pronto can be edited in place from a single Pronto editor (shared
  by the Sniffer, the Clipper, and device commands); a bound trigger re-points
  automatically when an edit changes the S/L fingerprint, and a carrier reading off
  the consumer standards can be snapped to the nearest one (30, 33, 36, 38, 40, or
  56 kHz). The Sniffer listens to IR receivers only: RF receivers that combined
  RF/IR hardware exposes on the infrared platform are excluded (RF support is
  roadmapped as an explicit opt-in), and the sniffed catalog is capped (200
  signals per remote, 20,000 total, oldest evicted first) so a noisy receiver
  cannot grow the store without bound.
- Clipper: a manual-entry surface (a third panel tab) for building virtual remotes by
  pasting Pronto hex codes, for cases where a live signal cannot be sniffed. Each
  pasted code is validated (hex shape, four-digit words, a learned-code 0000 header,
  burst-pair length math, and a carrier-frequency sanity warning) and then behaves
  identically to a sniffed signal: test, trigger, assign, or promote. Pasted signals
  share the same catalog as sniffed signals, distinguished by a source field
  (sniffed, manual, or plucked). Manual and plucked remotes are never auto-evicted. Pasting an identical
  code already on a remote is rejected, but genuinely different codes that share an
  S/L fingerprint are kept as separate signals via a byte-level tiebreaker. Remotes
  and their signals are drag-reorderable like the Sniffer's. The Create Remote
  dialog can also pick a known manufacturer and model from the device codebooks in
  the installed Home Assistant infrared library and materialize a remote pre-filled
  with one signal per button; it is a shortcut for the supported devices, not a
  universal lookup.
- Plucker: a vendor-code import surface (a capture tab parallel to the Sniffer and
  Clipper) that pulls IR codes already learned into a vendor blaster into HAIR as
  native signals, without re-learning each code at a receiver. HAIR registers a
  no-transmit observer emitter on HA's infrared platform (the HAIR Tweezer, an
  InfraredEmitterEntity), asks the vendor integration to replay a stored code by
  name through that emitter, and captures the resulting Command before it becomes
  physical IR. No IR is broadcast during a pluck. It works with any integration
  that can replay a stored code by name through a caller-chosen emitter; Tuya Local
  (send_learned_ir_command) is the first. New vendors are added as a single YAML
  file in custom_components/hair/pluckable/ with no HAIR code changes, validated
  against a versioned schema. The Plucker tab and a Blasters (Pluckable) section on
  the Devices page appear only when a compatible blaster is configured. Requires HA
  2026.6+, where the infrared platform exports InfraredEmitterEntity. Plucked
  signals share the same catalog as sniffed and clipped ones, distinguished by the
  source field.
- Mirror: a send-audit surface (the sixth panel tab, v0.6.6) logging every
  HA-originated IR transmission at send time, heard back or not. HAIR's own sends
  (device commands and catalog tests) are recorded with full identity and
  provenance; foreign sends from any integration on the infrared platform are
  caught via emitter state beacons (core writes the emitter's state on every
  platform send) and identified by their echo when a receiver hears one, or
  logged as a per-emitter "Unknown send" row when nothing does. Rows live in the
  shared signal catalog under a synthetic device (source "echo", fingerprint
  "hair-mirror") that the Sniffer filters out; they show the assignment or
  decoded identity, the emitter (friendly names), heard-by resolved to HA areas,
  a provenance chip (HAIR device / Catalog test / automation send / integration
  send), and send counts, and carry the standard Assign / Test / Trigger actions
  plus the code editor -- making the Mirror a universal TX tap: any vendor app
  send heard by a receiver is one Assign away from living in HAIR. Deliberately
  a log: no reorder, no clear-all, never auto-evicted; per-row delete clears an entry and the row resurrects on the next send of that identity. Echo
  attribution also gates triggers: a capture matching a pending send expectation
  (decoded identity or fingerprint, 2.5s TTL) is routed to the Mirror and never
  reaches the trigger or catalog pipeline, so triggers fire only on signals from
  outside Home Assistant and cannot feed back on HAIR's own output. The v0.4.0
  known-command suppression is removed (v0.6.6, "heard means shown"): assigned
  buttons keep flashing in the Sniffer and deleted rows resurrect on re-hearing;
  dismiss is the only hiding tool.
- Closet: portable code sets, called wigs (the fifth panel tab, before
  Mirror, v0.7.0). A wig is one JSON file (format "hair-wig/1", or
  "hair-wig/2" when it carries a climate state matrix; suffix
  .wig.json, documented in docs/wig-format.md): name, optional
  brand/model/notes/origin, and a signals list of alias + raw Pronto
  (+ ditto_count, bypass_protocol, and an optional send_count
  ride-along). Raw Pronto is the whole payload by design -- no
  decoded fields ship in the file, so importing decodes fresh against the
  installed decoders and a wig can never carry a stale identity. Optional
  kind (one lowercase word: "candles", "soundbar") and product identifiers
  (FCC ID, UPC, ASIN, verified-OEM anchors, single values or lists) keep
  off-brand hardware findable; closet search matches both (v0.8.0/0.8.1).
  Optional supersedes (v0.9.7): the wig's ancestry, wig ids newest-first,
  stamped automatically by Save as new (prepend source id onto source's
  own list, [source] alone when the source is not local, none from a
  from-scratch CREATE), capped at 16 both ends, bare string accepted as a
  one-element list, top-level metadata OUTSIDE every canonical form and
  digest. Supersession is declared by the successor, never marked on the
  ancestor. The drop bar reads it: an arriving wig whose ancestry names a
  wig already in the closet offers REPLACE (delete the old file, repoint
  every device sourced to the old id, optionally top up their missing
  buttons from the delta) over KEEP BOTH, the pair re-verified server-side
  in the executor so a stale confirm refuses rather than deleting the
  wrong file. Self-supersession (Save as new over one's own adopted wig)
  triggers the same flow from the save path.
  Files live in /config/hair/wigs/ (created at setup, outside the
  HACS-managed tree, scanned on demand); invalid files surface on the tab
  with field-level reasons
  instead of disappearing. The tab shelves library codebooks and local wigs
  together by brand; CLIP materializes a wig into a Clipper remote through the
  same import path as the code-library picker, and re-clipping collapses onto
  the existing remote. Built-in library rows (rendered from the
  infrared-protocols codes package) carry ADOPT and download alongside
  CLIP (v0.8.1); adopting one snapshots it into the closet as a wig
  (origin "library", deterministic render). Save to Closet on a HAIR
  device serializes it into the closet with an origin stamp
  (captured / clipped / plucked / device / library / converted:*) that the
  wig editor renders as a plain-English provenance sentence. The drop bar is
  also an import funnel: SmartIR JSON (all four encodings; climate files
  convert to state-matrix wigs, see below), Flipper Zero .ir (raw + parsed
  via library encoders), LIRC lircd.conf (raw codes + SPACE_ENC
  reconstruction), and Girr (IrScrutinizer's XML; ccf Pronto verbatim, raw
  synthesized, parameters-only skipped; any of the four spec root elements
  accepted since v0.7.1) all convert INTO
  wigs on drop, with skip reasons appended to the wig's notes -- one funnel,
  one-way doors. A Broadlink .storage scan and a CSV wizard remain planned.
  The Add picker intermixes local wigs into the library alphabet. HAIR
  ships zero codes: wigs are the landing spot for codes that cannot or have
  not yet gone upstream.
- Fittings (v0.8.0, remodeled 0.9.5 "The Fitting Room"): a wig is proven
  on real hardware and the proof travels with the file. Proving happens on
  the device: adopt the wig, live with it, and SAVE TO CLOSET (device
  header) presents a per-command checklist with a stateless TEST button per
  row; ticks become signed per-row claims. Each claim binds one row's
  transmit recipe by digest -- sha256(normalized_pronto + "|d<ditto>" +
  "|b<0|1>")[:16] -- so editing a row orphans exactly that row's claims and
  renames are free (alias and send_count are out of the digest,
  permanently). Exclusions are standardized verdicts, not failures:
  not_on_device / wont_work, offered on the authoring UI only for a
  matrix's dimension-checklist cells (v0.9.8, perfect-or-nothing) -- a
  lattice cannot be edited cell by cell the way commands can, so it keeps
  the valve; a flat wig's checklist is check-only, unchecked by default,
  and signing does not arm until every row carries a claim. Matrix bundles
  additionally pin cells_hash (never named content_hash; the legacy/claims
  discriminator is entry SHAPE, not the format stamp). Bundles are
  ed25519-signed (key = raw 32-byte pubkey, sig over the bundle minus sig,
  sorted keys, compact, UTF-8; the key is the install's only pseudonym --
  no HA identifier, raw or hashed, ever enters a wig). Wig-level verdicts
  are derived, never stored: complete = one bundle covering every row
  worked; perfect fit = complete with zero exclusions; coverage = the
  union. The closet check is perfect-or-nothing (v0.9.8, retiring the
  three-tier "scoped" middle): a row shows the perfect check or nothing,
  matching the download filename exactly. An incomplete bundle -- a
  matrix carrying exclusions, or an older file with a partial attestation
  from before the ruling -- still parses, still counts toward
  fitters/coverage, and still lists in the ledger as "Incomplete"; it just
  has no closet-tick state of its own any more. The download name is
  server-composed from the wig's OWN fields (download_filename in
  wig_format): brand-kind-model slugified, falling back to the name slug
  when the wig has no brand, with the tier as a hyphenated suffix from the
  wig's own claims (-perfect-fit, none for anything short of it) --
  hyphenated never dotted, because the old dotted suffix failed the
  shop's upload. The client no longer composes a name at all, so a closet
  row and its filename read the same claims and can never disagree. A
  comb-flagged cell used to join the matrix checklist as its own
  coordinate-named row (v0.9.8 through v0.12.1); since v0.14.0 flagged
  cells stay in the matrix and are resolved in the device's Needs
  attention block (see Detangle below), and a perfect fit refuses to sign
  while any finding on the device is open. The read-only ledger (via the
  fittings-count door on the save dialog) shows fitters, per-row verdicts,
  signature states, and orphaned claims. Pre-claims fittings are dropped
  on import with a receipt notice; they cannot become claims (a whole-file
  hash says nothing about which rows anybody proved).
- Replace (Smart Perm v0.9.1, moved to the device in 0.9.5): a command
  whose code is wrong gets repaired in the command editor -- paste a
  Pronto or LISTEN and capture one through a receiver; the heard code
  populates the box directly and nothing commits until save. Replacing a
  command's bytes resets its raw pin: the pin is a claim a specific
  capture earned, so the chip re-derives from the new bytes and the user
  re-pins deliberately. On a device adopted from a wig, SAVE TO CLOSET
  detects content differences and offers UPDATE: renames are matched
  pair-keyed (digest + alias, two-pass, guards the duplicate-payload
  case), content changes are proposed explicitly, the wig re-combs on the
  way out, and claims on unchanged rows survive by construction. The
  0.9.1 session bookkeeping (provenance markers, replaced_from, carry
  maps) is retired: nothing writes or reads it; old files carrying it are
  inert extra data.
- Bypass protocol (0.9.5): an optional per-signal boolean in the
  wig format, and a matching tx_force_raw knob on UnknownSignal, meaning "send
  these bytes verbatim, do not decode and re-encode". Motivated by GH #78: a
  Symphony repeat-train re-encodes to one clean frame and the device ignores
  it. Settable on a device command, a sniffed signal and a clipped signal;
  carried across assign, export, adopt and CLIP.
  IN the canonical signals hash but only when true, so every pre-existing wig
  and fitting signature stays byte-identical. The comb SKIPS bypassed rows in
  the shape checks and excludes them from the population that defines normal
  (a repeat-train would otherwise drag the median and condemn its honest
  siblings), and records the skip in the receipt -- but a bypassed row is a
  normal fitting checklist row, never an advisory one, so it still takes a
  verdict and counts toward completeness. Matrix cells do NOT carry it: the
  matrix send path is already an unconditional raw replay.
- Transmit recipe (Highlights): the wig states everything that goes on
  the wire. ditto_count is per-signal, always explicit, 0..20, IN the
  content hash (dittos change the waveform and the fitting transmits
  them); send_count is a carried ADVISORY, out of the hash, because the
  fitting has never transmitted the row's value -- the session control
  decides -- so no signature ever attested it. Canonical signal object
  is exactly {alias, pronto, ditto_count, bypass_protocol}, four keys,
  no conditional rules; cells drop send_count and carry no ditto field.
  Format major bumps to hair-wig/3 for BOTH kinds: a pure capability
  gate, so an older install refuses with a version message instead of
  reporting tamper on a good file. Bypass x ditto are mutually
  exclusive (the exporter writes 0 with a receipt; the comb raises an
  advisory on a hand-made file carrying both). Fitting transmit is
  max(row send_count, session send times) -- the row states the device
  floor, the session adds headroom and can never undercut it.
  _row_digest hashes the whole recipe (pronto|d<n>|b<0|1>), so a ditto
  tune returns that row to untested instead of carrying its old
  verdict. Tuning a ditto is async_tune, a separate door from
  async_replace: replace must keep refusing an identical pronto, and
  weakening that check would break the marker-implies-roll invariant
  Changed Codes rows depend on.
- TX knobs (0.9.5): send_count (whole-frame repetition) and
  repeat_count (NEC dittos) render through one component, ir-tx-knobs, on
  device command rows, Mirror rows, Sniffer signals and Clipper signals. The
  ditto glyph is suppressed on a bypassed row because raw replay never emits
  dittos. send_count is NOT a field on the Command: neither build_command nor
  build_decoded_command accepts one, and all three transmit paths keep it as a
  local loop bound, so every record_send call site passes it explicitly and an
  AST test in test_mirror.py fails if one stops. A Mirror row records the
  counts the send actually used, last-send semantics, defaulting to None so
  the echo-heard path cannot erase them.
- Decode trust (v0.14.2): every decoded identity carries a coverage
  verdict computed where the decode is minted (protocol_decode). A label
  must account for every frame of its capture -- the winning decoder's
  votes plus its repeat markers -- with two carve-outs: a repeat-voting
  decoder's discarded frames are forgiven when they are the same shape as
  the winner (jitter, preambles), and an NEC salvage forgives only
  within-frame doubt. The verdict persists as decode_covers on commands
  and signals (absent means not yet judged, and judged-absent recovers
  when a decoder library upgrade adds capability); both transmit sites
  replay raw when it is False, alongside the 0.14.1 matrix guard. The
  chip on an untrusted row is informational. All command-creating doors
  share one mint helper (mint.py) and device clone copies a pinned field
  roster. Codes shown to a person for copying carry a real trailing
  terminator via a derived code_export key (stored text and wig files
  keep the zero-gap canonical form).
- Row column discipline (0.9.5): the Sniffer's protocol chip,
  hit count, relative time and frequency sit in fixed centred cells, and the
  device detail's action badge reserves the widest label its device type can
  render. Sizing is a hidden copy of that label stacked in the same CSS grid
  cell as the visible one, so the browser settles the width in the live font
  and language; measurement (ir-device-detail._measureActionBadges) only picks
  a font tier. Measure from labels actually rendered, not from the option
  list: _getActionLabel falls back to the raw mapping key when a device
  carries a mapping from a type it no longer is.
- Combing (Smart Perm, v0.9.1): protocol-agnostic checks that a wig's codes
  agree with each other, in wig_comb.py -- field-versus-label and frame-integrity sweeps against twelve vendored field maps (v0.12.0, ratified fields only, map-driven frame splitting, hollow-comb coverage for unmapped wigs), repeat-frame self-consistency with the vote shown and a coverage block in the receipt (v0.11.0), frame-shape uniformity, partial row
  collapse, gaps in a captured temperature run, coordinate uniqueness, and
  duplicate-label groups (advisory only, never counted, never merged). Runs at
  import on every wig and on demand via wigs/comb (executor; 2,689-cell
  matrices are real). Never changes a code. The receipt rides wig.extra["comb"]
  outside every canonical hash, so combing cannot invalidate a fitting. A whole
  row collapsing to one code is CORRECT and never flagged; only a partial
  collapse is a defect. Strict frame-shape matching applies to lattices only:
  bi-phase protocols vary pair count by command, so flat remotes flag gross
  outliers instead. The closet row carries a comb glyph, grey with a yellow or
  red glow, which is also the action that opens the report.
- Detangle (v0.14.0): comb findings become fixes, in tangles.py behind the
  tangles/* websocket door. list_tangles turns a device's comb receipt into
  rows, one per flagged code, each carrying a plain reason line (fourteen
  reason keys; field-mismatch findings get the map's labels stamped on).
  Rows cluster into three roads. FIX: the correct bytes already exist in
  the file (a donor cell that reads as the needed value, or a frame
  synthesized under a ratified field rule and pre-read back before it is
  offered); the user accepts one or all. LISTEN: a press from the real
  remote is needed; the heard frame is read back against the coordinate
  and a mismatch is reported three times before Use It Anyway records a
  keep attestation. Since 0.14.1 the whole repair happens in one Fix
  window per row (Listen beside a paste box feeding the same gated
  apply; closing the window skips and records nothing), a press a
  map-covered wig cannot read climbs the same ladder instead of being
  accepted, and the repeat-disagreement check stands down when a
  repeat-voting decoder (SYMPHONY class) accepted the whole capture,
  with the receipt recording decode-resolved. DECIDE: two members carry one name or one code; rename,
  delete, or Keep Both. Attestations key on target, payload digest, and
  field-map version (flat rows on digest and version alone, so answers
  survive renames); an attested row reads clean on the surface and the
  record is kept, on the rule that a mark is an unanswered doubt. Every
  repair writes through to the closet as a repaired successor wig beside
  the original; the original is never edited. Comb stamps rederive at the
  moment a device comes clean. Matrix cells are never extracted as
  commands (the v0.9.8 porthole path is retired); flat-wig findings sit on
  the individual commands. A flat wig never gets synthesized bytes in
  this release: reconstruction by frame vote is next-cycle work. The
  Perfect Fit dialog refuses to open the checklist while findings are
  open and says how many codes need attention.
- Adopt Device (v0.8.1): every code set becomes a HAIR device in one step,
  from wherever you meet it. Closet wigs, library rows, Sniffer remotes,
  Clipper remotes, and Plucker blasters all carry one ADOPT button
  (it replaced the former Make HAIR Device / Promote action). A numbered dot
  shows how many HAIR devices already run those codes, with navigation to
  each. Adopting copies every signal as a named command with protocol
  identities stamped fresh and recognizable names auto-mapped to entity
  actions; the device type dropdown is seeded from the wig's kind. Adopting
  a wig-stamped Clipper remote flat passes a signpost first that names the
  source wig and offers adopting the wig instead (v0.8.8).
- Climate state matrices (v0.8.8, "Cold Cuts"): AC remotes do not send
  buttons, they send complete states, so HAIR models stateful climate
  devices as a matrix -- one complete Pronto code per mode / fan / swing /
  temperature combination. Dropping a SmartIR climate JSON on the closet
  converts it into a wig carrying the structured matrix (depth detected per
  branch; mode/fan/swing words kept verbatim; flat extras like sleep timers
  ride alongside as ordinary buttons). Matrix wigs write hair-wig/2 with an
  optional climate.unit field ("C" or "F", default "C", the SmartIR corpus
  convention); plain wigs stay hair-wig/1 so older installs keep reading
  them. ADOPT on a matrix wig creates a real climate entity: every
  user action resolves to exactly one cell (wig_climate.resolve_cell,
  nearest-temp snap, honest None on sparse branches -- HAIR never invents a
  cell) and transmits that cell's whole-state code. Swing and temperature
  controls appear only when the matrix carries those dimensions. The entity
  declares the file's native unit and HA converts the thermostat display;
  panel displays convert dynamically, while names minted from a cell (matrix
  clip, saved state commands) freeze in the install's unit at that moment.
  The matrix is stored as its own file next to the device
  (hair/matrices/<device_id>.matrix.json, matrix_store.py) so renaming a
  device never rewrites megabytes of Pronto. Fitting a matrix wig runs a
  dimension check (wig_climate.py): a deterministic 12-to-20-send checklist
  covering every mode, every fan speed, every swing position, and the
  temperature extremes -- each dimension proven along its own axis stands in
  for the lattice; it does not claim every cell was fired. The device detail
  page grows a state matrix card (browse the lattice, send a state, save it
  as a named command); CLIP on a matrix wig is gated behind a confirm that
  counts what it will mint. Stated limitations: Xiaomi-sourced Raw codes are
  refused (proprietary compression, not timing data), roughly half a percent
  of corpus cells skip with the reason written into the wig's notes, sparse
  matrices are honored, and files are treated as Celsius unless they say
  otherwise -- no unit guessing.
- Matrix Remotes and state listening (v0.10.0): a Remote made from a
  climate matrix wig or an AC device carries the STATE MATRIX card in
  listen mode -- no SEND on it by design, the handset is the test. A
  decoded press lights its mode / fan / swing / temperature coordinates
  together and leaves them marked, and a LAST HEARD row records the
  state, the time, and the receiver that heard it. Each heard state
  fires a hair_state_heard event carrying mode, fan, swing,
  temperature, power and receiver, and the Remote's HA device exposes a
  "State heard" device trigger over that event for automations that
  want any state rather than one cell; a single cell becomes an
  ordinary trigger from the card (+ Trigger, rendered with a STATE
  chip). Pinning an AC Remote to an AC Device re-sends every heard
  state through the Device's emitters.
- Climate presets from starred commands (v0.10.0): a star on each
  command row of an AC device promotes that command to preset_mode on
  the climate entity, named after the command; unstarring retires it.
  Learned commands and states saved out of the STATE MATRIX card both
  qualify; matrix cells do not. Presets are stored per device and
  are never written into a wig.
- Device-sent state (v0.10.1): every transmit path dispatches a
  device-sent notification once at least one emitter has accepted the
  send, carrying the device, the command and, for a climate device, the
  state coordinates that were sent. The climate entity derives its state
  from that notification, so a matrix send, a preset, a command row, a
  button entity and a pinned Remote's retransmit all move the thermostat
  card, while the entity's own service calls are tagged and ignored
  because the setter has already written the state. Coordinates travel
  structurally rather than being parsed back out of a display name:
  commands saved out of the STATE MATRIX card carry their own
  coordinates, stamped at mint and backfilled at setup against the
  device's current lattice. Nothing here reads state off the air; a
  heard state that is not a HAIR send never moves the card, and where a
  device has power monitoring the power verdict still resolves on/off.
- Store health (v0.10.1): HAIR watches Home Assistant's own store-write
  error log for its two stores, since HA's store writer logs a refused
  write rather than raising, and reports one warning and one
  self-clearing persistent notification per store that stops saving.
- Devices and Remotes (v0.10.0): the Devices tab carries two sections.
  DEVICES are HAIR device profiles, the things HAIR transmits to.
  REMOTES are handsets HAIR recognizes, and each Remote is a real Home
  Assistant device with a device_trigger entry per button, so a
  Remote's buttons appear by name in the automation editor's Device
  trigger list. HAIR Triggers, the pre-existing catch-all, is the first
  Remote in the section. A Remote owns its triggers permanently (they
  never move between Remotes) and can scope itself to a subset of
  receivers; only HAIR Triggers exposes a per-trigger receiver picker.
  Pinning binds a Remote to a Device: a press on the handset resolves
  to the matching command by signal identity and transmits it through
  that Device's emitters. The binding is many-to-many, one Remote to
  several Devices and one Device to several Remotes. HAIR never
  re-fires its own transmissions -- the Mirror's echo attribution
  already routes HAIR-originated captures away from the trigger
  pipeline -- so a pinned handset beside a receiver cannot loop; a loop
  breaker additionally cuts a single pairing for one minute and logs
  the Remote, Device and command if a pairing ever does run away,
  leaving the Remote's triggers firing throughout.
- Device Manager: lets users create profiles for IR-controlled devices (TVs, ACs,
  fans, lights, switches, screens, generic) with assigned IR emitters and learned
  commands. Assigning a sniffed or pasted signal copies it into the device as a
  command and leaves the source signal in the catalog, so one signal can be assigned
  to multiple devices or as multiple commands. Only delete, dismiss, and clear-all
  remove a signal. A device command can be renamed (its action mappings follow the
  new name) and given a send count so HAIR transmits the whole command more than once
  per press for a device that needs a repeat. The editor edits the command copy, not
  the catalog signal it came from.
- Entity Factory: automatically creates native HA entities based on device type --
  media_player, climate, fan, light, switch, cover, plus a universal remote entity
  for raw Pronto hex sending and a button entity for every learned command.
- Action Mapping: explicitly binds learned IR commands to HA entity features via a
  popover UI. A media_player only exposes volume control if commands are mapped to
  the volume actions, keeping entities clean and avoiding features the remote does
  not support.
- Trigger Manager: turns received IR signals into native HA event entities that
  fire hair_ir_command_received events. Any HA automation can consume them. A
  configurable min-hits threshold prevents accidental triggers from a single
  misfire. To the best of the project's knowledge, HAIR is the only HA integration
  turning received IR into automation triggers as of HA 2026.6.
  Location-aware (v0.5.7): the fire payload also carries receiver_entity_id plus
  receiver_area_id and receiver_area_name, resolved from the entity/device/area
  registry chain at fire time (so area renames and device moves need no migration).
  A trigger can carry a receiver_entity_ids scope list (empty = any receiver,
  backward compatible); scoped triggers fire only when a listed receiver observes
  the signal, and legacy ESPHome-bridge captures (receiver_entity_id=None) match
  only unscoped triggers. Multiple triggers per signal fingerprint are legal (one
  per room). A single press observed by several receivers fires each matching
  trigger once (per-trigger dedup over a sliding window) and counts as one hit
  toward min_hits.
  Tiered signal identity (v0.5.8): every "is this the same signal?" decision --
  trigger matching, the known-command matcher, Sniffer row dedup, repeat
  suppression, the Assign dot -- uses one tiered rule: decoded protocol identity
  when both sides have it, else the byte-level hash when both sides have it, else
  the coarse S/L fingerprint. The highest tier both sides carry decides; a tier
  only one side carries is skipped. Triggers store all three layers (null layers
  on pre-0.5.8 triggers = legacy-broad matching, so existing triggers are never
  narrowed; decoded identity is backfilled at load from the stored code, byte_hash
  deliberately is not). This matters on remotes whose buttons all share one S/L
  fingerprint because the protocol encodes bits in pulse widths below the
  short/long threshold -- Sony SIRC is the common case, alongside the
  Panasonic/Kaseikyo/TCL family -- and doubly on Sony, whose long mark sits
  exactly ON the classification threshold, so the same button's fingerprint can
  flip between captures: without the byte tier a trigger created for one button
  fires for every button, and without dropping the fingerprint-equality
  precondition the trigger then randomly misses its own button. The dedup window
  slides and is keyed per trigger, so protocols that transmit several full frames
  per press (Sony sends 4-5) count as one press even when frames flip fingerprints.
  Local-first decoders (v0.6.0): HAIR ships its own decoders for ten
  protocols -- Sony SIRC 12/15/20, RCA (v0.11.1, TCL Google TV and classic
  RCA handsets), Philips RC-6 modes 0 and 6A (v0.11.1, MCE and VU+ family), Symphony (8/12/16-bit rc_switch family),
  Philips RC-5 (incl. RC5X), Samsung32, Sharp, Kaseikyo (Panasonic family),
  Marantz Extended, and Nokia32 (Philips RC-MM, the Foxtel/Sky/Mediamaster
  set-top box family) -- in custom_components/hair/decoders/, each shaped
  exactly like an infrared_protocols module so it can be donated upstream as
  a near-file-copy. A registry in protocol_decode.py feature-detects per
  protocol: when the user's bundled infrared-protocols ships a decoder
  (from_raw_timings present), upstream wins; otherwise the local polyfill
  registers. Decoders split a capture into frames and majority-vote, so
  variable frame counts and receiver jitter cannot fragment one button into
  many identities (the v0.5.8 day-one field regression). The decoded
  fingerprint is formatted in exactly one place (format_fingerprint);
  bit-count variants fold into the protocol label (SONY15, KASEIKYO48,
  SYMPHONY12), Sharp/Marantz extension bits fold into a fingerprint suffix,
  and the RC-5/Marantz toggle bit is press STATE, stored in decoded_extras,
  excluded from identity, threaded into decoded TX, and flipped once per
  successful send. GE-AC registers identity-only (tx_rebuild=False): decoded
  identity matches/collapses signals, but TX always replays the captured
  raw, since re-encoding AC state risks transmitting wrong state.
  A Dyson decoder followed (beta v0.7.1, stable v0.7.2): Dyson fans
  rotate a mod-4 counter in every frame and reject a replayed value, so
  HAIR keeps device+button as the signal's identity (rotating presses
  collapse to one signal) and advances the counter on every send, from
  device commands and catalog Test presses alike.
  Recovery passes (v0.6.1): registry specs can carry optional seek and
  salvage hooks, wired for NEC today. Seek trims junk ahead of the main
  leader (stray repeat markers, partial bursts) before the strict decode;
  salvage runs only after a strict reject, re-reads data pulses by
  midpoint, and accepts solely on the protocol's own checksum. Samsung32
  additionally tolerates an end pulse fused with a replayed packet's
  leader (emitters that honor repeat_count on top of baked repeat frames
  leave no junction gap); its inverted-command checksum still gates.
  AC climate mapping (v0.6.1): commands named "Temp N" on an AC device
  auto-map to temp_N and derive temperature_presets (deduped, sorted);
  deleting one retires the preset. The climate entity seeds its target
  from the median preset so the thermostat dial has a handle, and
  reports the installation's temperature unit rather than a hardcoded
  scale.
  Tolerant match for file-sourced codes (v0.10.0): a code that entered
  HAIR from a file (a Closet wig, a Clipper paste, a Plucker pull)
  never passed through a receiver, so it carries none of the timing
  skew a given receiver adds and the exact tiers above can miss a real
  press of the handset it came from. When every exact tier misses AND
  the stored side is file-sourced, HAIR falls back to a normalized
  signal-shape comparison, which tolerates that skew. It applies to
  nothing else: receiver-learned codes, and codes carrying a decoded
  protocol identity, match exactly as they always have. Triggers and
  Remotes built from file-sourced codes, and pin resolution on a device
  adopted from a wig, are the paths this reaches.

Signal fingerprinting details:
- Uses S/L (short/long) pulse-duration classification. Each pulse is classified as
  short or long, producing a pattern that identifies the signal regardless of minor
  timing jitter between presses. Protocols whose long pulse falls just below the S/L
  threshold (such as the Panasonic and TCL families) are separated by an additional
  byte-level tiebreaker so distinct commands are not merged.
- Patterns are rendered as two-tone diamond sequences in the UI for visual ID.
- Covers all major consumer IR protocols: NEC, Samsung, JVC, LG, Sony, RC-5, RC-6.
- Source-remote grouping keys a NEW capture on the decoded identity (protocol
  plus address) whenever it decodes, and falls back to carrier frequency and
  preamble fingerprinting when it does not, so the Sniffer still groups signals
  it cannot read. A signal already in the catalog is filed with its existing
  row instead, found through a constant-time identity index, so no existing
  row, group, name or promotion is ever moved by a press; deleting a row is the
  user-controlled re-file.
- When a captured signal can be read as a known protocol (NEC plus the
  registry protocols above, Dyson included), HAIR also
  stores the decoded identity alongside the raw timings as a cache layer. Raw
  timings stay the source of truth; the decoded form gives stronger matching and
  lets transmit re-encode clean timings instead of replaying captured ones.
- The decoded form drives every transmit path consistently: device commands, the
  catalog-signal Test button (Sniffer, Clipper, Plucker), and the guided Capture
  save all prefer the re-encoded clean timings when a decoded identity is present.
  Assigning a signal and saving a captured command carry that identity onto the new
  command at creation time, not just at the next load.
- Two user-tunable TX knobs, editable on catalog signals, device commands, and
  the assign dialog: Ditto count (the NEC repeat-frame count appended after the
  main frame, for receivers that need a held-key pattern) and Send times
  (whole-frame retransmissions). The catalog-signal Test path honors both,
  matching device TX. The Ditto count input and chip honor the per-command
  NEC/PRONTO toggle and the signal's decoded state: when a command is set to
  PRONTO transmit (tx_force_raw) or a signal has no decoded protocol, the chip
  and the matching editor / assign-dialog input all hide, since dittos do not
  fire on the raw TX path.
- At capture, NEC dittos that follow a main frame are observed (single-anchor
  attribution with a 1.0s window and a 250ms inter-frame gate, max-merged) and
  surfaced in the signal editor as a read-only "Observed at capture" hint. The
  observation does not auto-set the TX Ditto count; the user acts on it.

Supported capture providers (auto-discovered):
- Native InfraredReceiverEntity instances (HA 2026.6+, hardware-agnostic;
  ESPHome receivers and SMLIGHT Ultima receivers ship this today)
- ESPHome devices with the remote_receiver component (legacy bridge)

Supported transmit hardware: any IR emitter exposed to HA's infrared platform,
including ESPHome IR LEDs, Tuya Local IR blasters, Broadlink RM series, and
SMLIGHT SLZB devices. One unavailable emitter no longer fails a multi-emitter
send (v0.8.0): sends succeed when at least one emitter fires, known-down
emitters are skipped, and only an all-emitters failure errors; a dead emitter
raises one self-replacing persistent notification naming the blaster and the
reason, dismissed automatically when it answers again (v0.8.1). RC-5 toggle
and Dyson counter state advance when at least one send lands.

Supported device types and resulting HA entities:
- Media Player -> media_player (power, volume, mute, source, channels, navigation, transport)
- AC -> climate (two modes: preset-based from mapped commands, or
  matrix-based full state control when adopted from a climate matrix wig)
- Fan -> fan (power, speed stepping or direct speed levels 1-10, oscillate)
- Light -> light (on/off, brightness stepping)
- Switch -> switch (on/off)
- Screen -> cover (open, close, stop)
- Other -> remote (generic IR command sender)

Localization (v0.6.8): the panel and the config flow ship in ten languages
(en, es, fr, ja, de, pl, pt/pt-BR, nl, it, ru). The panel follows the HA user's
profile language with English fallback. Non-English locales are
programming-assistant drafts, marked "reviewer wanted" inside each
dictionary file (the Spanish panel translation is native-speaker
reviewed as of v0.8.0); native-speaker reviews
and new languages are welcome as small PRs guarded by parity tests (see
CONTRIBUTING.md, "Adding a language").

Every device also gets a remote entity for raw Pronto hex codes and a button entity
per learned command for direct dashboard or automation access.

Requirements:
- Home Assistant 2026.4 or later (introduces the native infrared platform that HAIR
  depends on)
- Python 3.12+
- At least one IR transmitter or receiver supported by HA's infrared platform

What HAIR is NOT:
- Not a replacement for the Broadlink or ESPHome integrations -- HAIR complements
  them. The underlying IR hardware integrations are still required.
- Not a replacement for HA's infrared platform -- HAIR is an admin layer on top of
  the platform.
- Not compatible with Home Assistant versions earlier than 2026.4 (the infrared
  platform did not exist before then).
- Not a YAML-based integration -- all device profiles and command assignments are
  managed through the sidebar UI.
- Not a built-in Home Assistant integration -- must be installed via HACS as a
  custom repository. (HAIR passes Home Assistant's hassfest checks as of
  v0.7.2, clearing the requirements for HACS default-store listing.)

Receiver architecture:
- On HA 2026.6+, HAIR uses the native InfraredReceiverEntity API
  (infrared.async_subscribe_receiver) for hardware-agnostic signal capture.
- On HA 2026.4-2026.5, HAIR falls back to the legacy ESPHome event bus bridge
  (esphome.remote_received events) automatically.
- Both paths convert signals to Pronto hex at the entry point for consistent
  fingerprinting.

## Repositories

- [HAIR (this repo)](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR): Python HACS integration
  (custom_components/hair/), TypeScript frontend panel served at /hair, HACS
  metadata (hacs.json), and project documentation.

## Documentation

- [README](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR/blob/main/README.md): Full feature
  overview, why-HAIR rationale, entity platform reference, Devices tab and Sniffer
  tab walkthroughs, installation and setup, and architecture diagram. Truncated
  translated READMEs (README.es.md, README.fr.md, README.ja.md, README.de.md,
  README.pl.md, README.pt.md, README.nl.md, README.it.md, README.ru.md) sit at the
  repo root, each carrying the pitch, install steps, and a pointer back to the full
  English documentation; they are drafted by a programming assistant, refreshed
  each release, and open for native-speaker ownership.
- [info.md](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR/blob/main/info.md): HACS short-form
  summary shown in the HACS UI during install.
- [The wig format](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR/blob/main/docs/wig-format.md):
  the portable code-set file format (hair-wig/1 and hair-wig/2), including the
  climate state-matrix block, fittings, and the canonical hash forms.
- [Making your integration pluckable](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR/blob/main/docs/making-your-integration-pluckable.md):
  guide for HA integration authors on exposing the cross-emitter replay service the
  Plucker needs. The registry file format is documented in
  custom_components/hair/pluckable/README.md.
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md): Release
  history.
- [CONTRIBUTING](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md):
  Contribution guidelines, including the requirement that llms.txt be updated
  alongside README changes (per DAB-LABS LLMDO release protocol).

## Hardware configurations

- [esphome/](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR/tree/main/esphome):
  Curated, HAIR-tested ESPHome configurations for common IR hardware. Each
  config carries a machine-readable header (device, GPIO map, tested versions,
  contributor) for easy discovery. Two-tier convention per device: minimal
  (just the IR pieces) and full (preserves device-specific features like touch
  pads and status LEDs).

## Releases

- [Releases](https://github.com/DAB-LABS/HAIR/releases): Versioned releases. HACS
  installs from tagged releases.

## Optional

- [DAB-LABS](https://github.com/DAB-LABS): Other open-source Home Assistant and
  homelab projects by the same author, including SMART Sniffer (disk health
  monitoring) and esphome-ld2411s (mmWave presence sensor component).
The Plucker also reads learned-code stores other integrations persist in Home Assistant storage (Broadlink, Tuya Local; pluckable mechanism: storage), importing named commands read-only, with canonical re-encode where codes decode.
